PPC. Now, PPC stands for pay-per-click, where

on his channel. But he's also got this amazing 
Amazon FBA course, the Passion Product Formula,

So, there's a link in the description, so you

in net profits. This year, I learned that product 
quality and customer satisfaction are absolutely

everything. After our first year, we immediately 
started working on improvements for our product

drafttop. Every single review became a blueprint 
for making our product better. We spent $30 to

$40,000 a year annually just to keep improving the

The first year was like watching your child take 
their first steps to flat out sprinting. Year one

was good, but in year two, things blew up faster 
than I could imagine. A big reason for this was

our appearance on Shark Tank in February of 2021. 
That national TV exposure introduced our product

to millions of people and our sales went through

waking up every morning and seeing thousands 
of dollars come in overnight. The feeling was

breathtaking. After years of people questioning 
whether this can opener thing would actually work,

my third year selling on Amazon. And after taking

This was the year everything truly exploded. We 
refined our product, dialed in our marketing,

and built a loyal customer base. The momentum 
felt unstoppable, and I really felt like I was

dreaming every day. Going into our fourth year, 
we set our sights on breaking the million-doll

mark on Amazon. And we started expanding our 
product line with complimentary items. So,

with my fourth year on Amazon, I've made over 
a million dollars in revenue. But remember,

revenue is not profit. After taking out all of my 
expenses, advertising, and other fees, I'm only

left with a net $443,000 and profit. This really 
felt incredible. Breaking the million-doll mark

on Amazon alone was something I never imagined, 
especially after tinkering with prototypes in

my garage back in 2011. My hands would actually 
shake when I opened the dashboard each morning

and saw the million plus dollars. And not from 
nervousness, but pure adrenaline. What makes

this more incredible was thinking about how close 
I came to not actually starting this business.

I almost stayed in my comfortable insurance job, 
almost gave up in that four-year period, and also

almost just settled for selling on my website. The 
journey of selling Draft Top on Amazon has become

an emotional roller coaster. But it just goes to 
show that as long as you keep taking action and

start swinging that axe forever, you can make 
money on Amazon. You really only lose when you

give up. There's just one catch to my story of 
selling Draft Top on Amazon. Although I made over

$2.7 million on Amazon, I could have made millions 
more if I avoided these three mistakes. So,

pay attention. My first big mistake was poor tax 
planning. And this mistake cost me over $40,000.

After our first Kickstarter campaign, we had over 
$80,000 in true profit, but didn't do any tax

planning. When tax season came around, we had to 
pay nearly 40% of that in taxes. Money that could

have been reinvested into the business. We should 
have worked with a tax professional which could

have identified legitimate business expenses that 
would have reduced that tax penalty. And this was

a painful lesson in financial management. What you 
can learn from this is don't wait until tax season

to learn about taxes. Work with a tax professional 
early on to structure your business finances

properly. Legitimate business expenses like 
marketing, product improvement, or inventory can

actually help reduce your taxable income all while 
growing your business. My second mistake, wasting

money on expensive sponsorships. And this cost 
me over $300,000. After the tax planning mistake,

we swung too far in the opposite direction. We 
decided to spend a lot of money on sponsorships

to avoid paying tax on our profits. We spent 
around $300,000 on bar stool sports and NASCAR

sponsorships thinking that they would generate 
awareness and sales, but our product requires

demonstration and explanation. So just having 
our name mentioned on a billboard or on a stadium

did not convert to sales. So we only saw about 
$100,000 in return from that $300,000 investment.

is created equal. So understand how your specific

product needs to be marketed. For products 
that require demonstration or explanation,

invest in content that shows your product in 
action other than passive brand awareness. So test

marketing channels with smaller investments before 
making larger spends. And our third mistake,

the biggest mistake was avoiding and delaying 
our Amazon launch. This mistake cost me over

a million dollars. The most costly mistake was 
waiting until 2020 to launch on Amazon. After our

first Kickstarter in 2015, we spend the next four

in late 2020. Our sales finally exploded. If we

millions of customers actively searching for
